# What Is a Go-to-Market Strategy?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-go-to-market-strategy/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-15 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A go-to-market strategy sets out how a company reaches and wins customers at a cost that leaves a business. lowob treats it as four decisions that must agree: who exactly, what they must believe, how trust moves, and what evidence proves it. Buyer research shows why the third has become harder: buyers use more channels and many prefer to buy without a seller.

A go-to-market (GTM) strategy is the plan for how a company finds customers, persuades them to buy and does so at a cost that leaves a profitable business. **lowob** treats it as four decisions that must agree with each other: who exactly the buyer is, what they must believe, how trust moves from first contact to contract, and what evidence will show it is working. A list of channels and campaigns is not a GTM strategy; it is a list of tactics.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What a go-to-market strategy means

The term covers the commercial choices that sit between having a product and having revenue. Gartner's framework for sales leaders defines it as "a plan that details how an organization can engage with customers" and names five components: target market identification, the first customer touchpoint, sales compensation planning, corporate investments and voice of the customer.

**lowob**'s working definition, set out in [What Go-to-Market Means](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-gtm-for-founders/), groups the choices into four decisions. Each constrains the others.

| Decision | Question it answers | Evidence it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who, exactly | Which narrowly defined buyers have the costliest version of the problem, the authority and budget to fix it, and a reason to act now? | Win rates and sales cycle by segment |
| What they must believe | What change does the buyer want, in their own language? | Buyers repeat the message back; loss reasons shift |
| How trust moves | What is the path from first contact to signed contract: self-serve, sales-led, partner-led or community-led? | Conversion and cost at each step of the path |
| What proves it | Which few numbers will show the strategy is working, and by when? | Agreed targets, reviewed on a fixed rhythm |

A GTM strategy is not the same as a marketing plan, a sales target or a product launch. Those are parts of it. The strategy is the agreement between the parts.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

### Buyers have changed the path

The third decision, how trust moves, has become harder. McKinsey's B2B Pulse survey of nearly 4,000 decision makers, published in September 2024, found buyers used an average of ten channels in their buying journey, up from five in 2016. It also found a "rule of thirds": at each stage, roughly a third of buyers prefer in-person contact, a third remote contact and a third digital self-service.

Gartner's survey of 632 B2B buyers, run in August and September 2024, found 61% prefer an overall rep-free buying experience. The same research found 73% avoid suppliers who send irrelevant outreach. A strategy that assumes every buyer wants a sales call, or that more outbound volume will compensate for a weak fit, now fails faster.

### Tactics without a strategy waste money

Without the four decisions written down, each team picks its own. Marketing targets one segment, sales chases another and partners bring a third. Spending rises while win rates stay flat. **lowob**'s piece on [strategy versus tactics](https://lowob.com/research/gtm-strategy-vs-tactics/) sets out the symptoms in more detail.

> A go-to-market strategy is four choices that agree. Change one and the other three must be checked.

### Agents need it written down

AI agents in sales and marketing amplify whatever strategy they are given. An outbound agent pointed at a loose ideal customer profile sends more messages to the wrong people, faster. In **lowob**'s model, the GTM choices belong in the decision record, with a reason, owner and expected outcome, so agents and people read the same version.

## How to test your go-to-market strategy

| Test | Question to ask the leadership team | Warning sign |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single buyer | Can three leaders describe the target buyer in the same words? | Three different answers |
| Narrowness | Could a seller name ten real accounts that fit, today? | "Mid-market companies" |
| Belief | Do win-loss interviews repeat your message? | Buyers cite price or relationships only |
| Primary motion | Is one path primary, with others in support? | Every channel funded equally |
| Economics | Do you know the cost to acquire a customer through the main path? | Nobody owns the number |
| Review | When did the strategy last change because of evidence? | Never, or every month |

Firms between 20 and 500 people usually run more than one motion. That is workable if one is primary and the others support it. [Product-Led vs Sales-Led vs Partner-Led Growth](https://lowob.com/research/product-led-vs-sales-led-vs-partner-led/) covers how to choose.

## lowob takeaways

- **Four decisions.** Who, what they must believe, how trust moves and what proves it.
- **They must agree.** A new segment means a new message, path and set of measures.
- **The path is harder.** Buyers use more channels and many prefer to buy without a seller.
- **Write it down.** Recorded choices keep teams, and agents, working from one version.
